misconceptions.statement: A resistor uses up current, so less current comes out than goes in.
misconceptions.correction: The same current flows into and out of a resistor. What drops across it is the voltage: the resistor turns electrical energy into heat.

scenes.title: Ohm's law
scenes.subtitle: How voltage, current and resistance are linked

beats.narration: Welcome! In this short lecture we look at Ohm's law, the rule that links voltage, current and resistance in a circuit.
By the end, you will be able to state the law, use it to find a current, and read a resistance from a graph.

intent.goal: Open the lecture and set out what students will be able to do.

beats.narration: A simple circuit has three quantities that work together. Voltage is the push that drives charge around the circuit, and it is measured in volts.
Current is how much charge flows past a point each second. It is measured in amperes.
Resistance tells us how strongly a part opposes that flow. It is measured in ohms.
Ohm's law links all three: voltage equals current times resistance.
So for a fixed resistor, if you double the voltage, the current doubles as well. A graph of voltage against current is a straight line, and its slope is the resistance.

side_panel.title: Voltage against current, 4 Ω resistor
side_panel.rationale: A straight line through the origin shows that current is proportional to voltage; its slope is the resistance.

intent.goal: Define voltage, current and resistance and state Ohm's law.

board.text: The electrical [[push]] that drives charge, in volts.
How strongly a part [[opposes]] the flow, in ohms (Ω).
Double the voltage and the current doubles too.

beats.narration: Let's use the law. A room heater is connected to a 230 volt supply, and its element has a resistance of 46 ohms. What current does it draw?
We want the current, so we rearrange the formula: current equals voltage divided by resistance.
Now put in the values. Pause here and try the division yourself.
230 divided by 46 is 5, so the heater draws 5 amperes.
Always check the units: volts divided by ohms gives amperes, so the answer makes sense.

intent.goal: Model how to rearrange V = I R and find a current.
key_points: Check the units of the answer

board.text: Given: V = 230 V and R = 46 Ω
board.justification: Read the values from the question
Divide both sides of V = I R by R

board.text: Check the units: volts ÷ ohms = amperes.

scenes.title: Your turn

beats.narration: Your turn. A 12 volt battery is connected across a 3 ohm resistor. What current flows? Choose an answer before the timer runs out.

intent.goal: Check that students can recall the law and apply I = V / R.

scenes.question: A 12 V battery is connected across a 3 Ω resistor. What current flows?
feedback_wrong: That is voltage times resistance, as if a bigger resistance let more current through. Current is voltage divided by resistance.
That is resistance divided by voltage. Turn the fraction the other way up.
Adding the numbers does not give a current. Use I = V / R.

reveal_beats.narration: The answer is 4 amperes. Current equals voltage divided by resistance, and 12 divided by 3 is 4.

beats.narration: Let's sum up. Voltage pushes, current flows, and resistance opposes the flow.
Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance, so current is voltage divided by resistance.
For a fixed resistor, the current is proportional to the voltage.
And remember: a resistor does not use up current. The same current flows in and out; the voltage drops across it as energy turns into heat.

side_panel.title: What you learned
side_panel.rationale: Shows how Ohm's law builds on voltage, current and resistance.

intent.goal: Summarise the law and correct the most common misconception.

board.text: Ohm's law: V = I R, so I = V / R.
For a fixed resistor, current is proportional to voltage.

board.justification: The same current flows in and out; the voltage drops across the resistor as energy turns into heat.

key_formulas.name: Ohm's law
key_formulas.description: Voltage across a resistor equals the current through it times its resistance.

definitions.definition: The electrical push that drives charge around a circuit, measured in volts (V).
The rate at which charge flows past a point, measured in amperes (A).
How strongly a component opposes the flow of charge, measured in ohms (Ω).

practice_problems.question: A torch bulb has a resistance of 6 Ω and is connected to a 3 V battery. Find the current through the bulb.
steps: Write the law for current: I = V / R
hints: Current is voltage divided by resistance.

practice_problems.question: A current of 2 A flows through a resistor when 10 V is applied across it. What is its resistance, and what current flows if the voltage is raised to 15 V?
steps: Rearrange the law: R = V / I
With 15 V: I = 15 V / 5 Ω = 3 A
practice_problems.final_answer: R = 5 Ω; the current becomes 3 A.
hints: Find the resistance first; it does not change.
Then use I = V / R with the new voltage.
